_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Portugal covering Lusitanian/Roman Lusitania, Visigothic kingdom, Moorish conquest (711-1139), Reconquista (Afonso Henriques 1139, first king), Age of Discovery (15th-16th century, Vasco da Gama, Brazil, Magellan circumnavigation), Iberian Union with Spain (1580-1640), 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Napoleonic invasion, Brazilian independence 1822, constitutional monarchy, First Republic 1910, Estado Novo dictatorship (Salazar 1933-74), Carnation Revolution 1974, EU 1986.

religion.note: Historically deeply Catholic; Fátima (Marian apparition 1917, major pilgrimage site); declining practice (especially youth); church attendance ~20%; colonial missionary tradition (spread Portuguese/Catholicism to Brazil, Africa, Asia); 1974 democratic revolution separated church-state

ethnic_groups.name: Portuguese
ethnic_groups.notes: Iberian/Celtic/Roman/Germanic/Moorish mix; regional identities (northern vs southern, Algarve, Azores, Madeira); 'saudade' (melancholic longing, national sentiment); fado music (UNESCO); massive emigration history (diaspora ~5M, 'Portuguese don't say goodbye, they leave'); retornados (1M+ returned from African colonies 1974-76)

ethnic_groups.name: Brazilian
ethnic_groups.notes: Largest immigrant group (~230k); language/culture shared; economic migration both directions; colonial legacy

ethnic_groups.name: African Portuguese-speaking
ethnic_groups.notes: Cape Verdean (~45k, long-established), Angolan (~28k), Guinea-Bissauan, Mozambican, São Toméan; colonial legacy; retornados descendants; recent immigration

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Romanian, Chinese, British (retirees, Algarve), French, Indian (Goan); African communities (Cape Verde historically most integrated); Roma; Sephardic Jewish heritage (expelled 1497, crypto-Jews, recent citizenship law 2015-2022 for descendants)

independence.from: Kingdom of León (Battle of Ourique, Afonso Henriques proclaimed king); internationally recognised 1143 (Treaty of Zamora)

country_profile.notes_unique: Age of Discovery (Era dos Descobrimentos, 15th-16th century, first global maritime empire: Vasco da Gama reached India 1498, Brazil 1500, Macau 1557, Malacca; Magellan circumnavigation 1519-22; Prince Henry the Navigator/Infante Dom Henrique; Padrão Portuguese stone markers worldwide); Portuguese language (250M+ speakers, 6th most spoken, official language 9 countries across 4 continents); 1755 Lisbon earthquake (60,000 dead, All Saints' Day tsunami, destroyed city, Marquês de Pombal rebuilt); Carnation Revolution (Revolução dos Cravos, April 25, 1974, bloodless military coup ended 48-year dictatorship, spontaneous people power, red carnations in gun barrels, freed African colonies); Estado Novo (Salazar 1933-68, authoritarian corporatist, world's longest-ruling dictator at time, colonial wars bankrupted country); fado music (UNESCO, melancholic, Amália Rodrigues); saudade (untranslatable Portuguese word, deep longing/nostalgia); Portuguese empire (1415-1999, longest European colonial empire, 600 years, Macau last to go 1999); 2008-14 troika bailout (€78B, austerity, emigration surge); Cristiano Ronaldo (most-followed person on social media, national icon); cork (produces 50% of world's cork, Alentejo oak forests); Port wine (Douro Valley, UNESCO)

comparative_rankings._note: Country position relative to continent and global. 'rank' = 1 is best/largest.

current_leader.name: Luís Montenegro
current_leader.title: Prime Minister
current_leader.notes: PSD (Social Democrats, centre-right); coalition with CDS-PP; won March 2024 snap election after Costa resignation; minority government; economist background; austerity-lite; corruption cleanup messaging

head_of_state.name: Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa
head_of_state.title: President
head_of_state.notes: PSD; law professor, journalist; 'President Marcelo' (informal, accessible); two terms; hugely popular; hugs everyone ('Marcelo hug'); COVID symbol of national unity; presidential powers used moderately; term ends 2026

former_leaders.name: António Costa
former_leaders.notes: PS (Socialist); Goan-Catholic father, Jewish mother; geringonça ('contraption', left-wing alliance); economic recovery from troika austerity; tourism boom; 8 years; resigned November 2023 (corruption investigation, lithium concessions, though not personally charged); popular until scandal

former_leaders.name: Pedro Passos Coelho
former_leaders.notes: PSD; austerity PM (troika conditions); youth emigration surge; unpopular but stabilized finances; defeated by Costa

former_leaders.name: José Sócrates
former_leaders.notes: PS; presided over financial collapse; troika bailout 2011; corruption charges 2014 (Operation Marquês, largest trial in Portuguese history, acquitted some charges, convicted others); damaged PS reputation

former_leaders.name: Mário Soares
former_leaders.notes: PS founder; opposition leader under dictatorship (exiled); democracy's founding father; first freely-elected PM; first civilian president in 60 years; EU accession 1986; died 2017 aged 92; 'Father of Democracy'

former_leaders.name: António de Oliveira Salazar
former_leaders.notes: Estado Novo (New State); corporatist authoritarian; devout Catholic; isolated Portugal ('proudly alone'); colonial wars (Angola/Mozambique/Guinea, unwinnable, bankrupted state); stroke 1968; world's longest-ruling dictator at retirement; complex legacy (stability vs authoritarianism); influenced by papal social teaching

910.name: Lusitanians & Roman Lusitania
910.description: The Lusitanians, a fierce Celtic-Iberian people, resisted Roman conquest under the legendary Viriathus. Rome eventually prevailed and created the province of Lusitania, whose capital Emerita Augusta lay just across the modern border, while cities like Olisipo (Lisbon) and Conimbriga flourished.

sub_clusters.name: Lusitanian Resistance & Viriathus
sub_clusters.description: The Castro culture hill-forts, Celtic and pre-Celtic peoples of western Iberia, and Viriathus's guerrilla war against Rome—one of the most celebrated resistance campaigns of antiquity.
key_events: Viriathus leads Lusitanian resistance against Rome (147–139 BCE)

sub_clusters.name: Roman Lusitania & Urbanisation
sub_clusters.description: Augustus's creation of the province of Lusitania, the romanisation of Olisipo (Lisbon) and Conimbriga, road networks, early Christianity, and the impact of Germanic invasions (Suebi, Visigoths).

920.name: Suebi, Visigoths & Moorish Conquest
920.description: The Suebi established a kingdom in Gallaecia and northern Lusitania, later absorbed by the Visigoths. The Umayyad conquest of 711 brought Islamic rule to most of the peninsula, setting the stage for centuries of Reconquista.

sub_clusters.name: Suebi Kingdom & Visigothic Absorption
sub_clusters.description: The Suebi kingdom centred on Braga (the first Germanic people to convert to Catholicism), Visigothic conquest, and the cultural blend of Roman, Germanic, and Hispano-Celtic traditions.

sub_clusters.name: Moorish Iberia & Early Reconquista
sub_clusters.description: The Umayyad conquest, Islamic al-Gharb (Algarve), and the beginning of the Christian Reconquista from the northern mountains of Asturias-León, including the Presúria of Portucale (868).
key_events: Presúria of Portucale – Vímara Peres reconquers and repopulates Porto (868)

920.name: County & Kingdom of Portugal
920.description: From the County of Portucale, Afonso Henriques forged an independent kingdom recognised by the papacy in 1179. The Reconquista pushed south, culminating in the capture of the Algarve and making Portugal one of Europe's earliest defined nation-states.

sub_clusters.name: County of Portucale & Afonso Henriques
sub_clusters.description: Henry of Burgundy's county, the Battle of São Mamede (1128) establishing Afonso Henriques's authority, the Battle of Ourique (1139), and the Treaty of Zamora recognising Portuguese independence (1143).
key_events: Treaty of Zamora – Castile recognises Portuguese independence (1143)

sub_clusters.name: Reconquista South & Conquest of the Algarve
sub_clusters.description: The capture of Lisbon (1147) with Crusader help, the Military Orders (Templars, Hospitallers, Order of Aviz), and the completion of the Reconquista with the conquest of the Algarve (1249).
key_events: Siege and capture of Lisbon with Crusader assistance (1147)

930.name: Age of Discovery & Maritime Empire
930.description: Portugal pioneered the Age of Discovery under Henry the Navigator, Vasco da Gama, and Pedro Álvares Cabral. Portuguese explorers established the first global maritime empire, connecting Europe, Africa, Asia, and Brazil in an unprecedented network of trade and colonisation.

sub_clusters.name: Henry the Navigator & Atlantic Exploration
sub_clusters.description: The conquest of Ceuta (1415), Prince Henry's school of navigation at Sagres, the discovery of Madeira and the Azores, the rounding of Cape Bojador (1434), and the beginning of the African slave trade.
key_events: Conquest of Ceuta – beginning of the Age of Discovery (1415)
Gil Eanes rounds Cape Bojador, breaking the 'Sea of Darkness' barrier (1434)

sub_clusters.name: Vasco da Gama & Pedro Álvares Cabral
sub_clusters.description: Bartolomeu Dias rounding the Cape of Good Hope (1488), Vasco da Gama's sea route to India (1498), Pedro Álvares Cabral's discovery of Brazil (1500), and the Treaty of Tordesillas dividing the world with Spain.
key_events: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut, India (20 May 1498)
Cabral discovers Brazil (22 April 1500)

sub_clusters.name: Global Empire & Manueline Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: The Estado da Índia controlling the Indian Ocean spice trade, Afonso de Albuquerque's conquests (Goa, Malacca, Hormuz), the Manueline architectural style, Luís de Camões's Os Lusíadas, and the empire's overextension.
key_events: Albuquerque conquers Goa for Portugal (1510)

930.name: Iberian Union & Restoration of Independence
930.description: The death of King Sebastião at Alcácer Quibir (1578) and the subsequent succession crisis led to sixty years of Spanish Hapsburg rule. The Restoration War of 1640 re-established Portuguese independence under the House of Braganza.

sub_clusters.name: Alcácer Quibir & Iberian Union
sub_clusters.description: King Sebastião's catastrophic defeat at Alcácer Quibir (1578), the myth of Sebastianism, Philip II of Spain's takeover, and sixty years of dual monarchy eroding Portuguese colonial power.
key_events: King Sebastião killed at Battle of Alcácer Quibir (1578)

sub_clusters.name: Restoration War & House of Braganza
sub_clusters.description: The 1 December 1640 coup restoring Portuguese independence under João IV of Braganza, the Restoration Wars against Spain (1640–68), and the rebuilding of Portugal's colonial and diplomatic networks.
key_events: Portuguese Restoration – Duke of Braganza proclaimed King João IV (1 Dec 1640)

940.name: Lisbon Earthquake & Pombaline Reform
940.description: The catastrophic 1755 Lisbon earthquake killed tens of thousands and reshaped European thought. The Marquis of Pombal's radical rebuilding and Enlightenment reforms transformed Portugal but created an authoritarian precedent.

sub_clusters.name: Great Lisbon Earthquake (1755)
sub_clusters.description: The devastating earthquake, tsunami, and fire of 1 November 1755, killing an estimated 30,000–50,000 people, Pombal's rational response, the rebuilding of the Baixa Pombalina, and the impact on Enlightenment philosophy (Voltaire's Candide).
key_events: Great Lisbon Earthquake devastates the city (1 Nov 1755)

sub_clusters.name: Pombaline Reforms & Enlightenment
sub_clusters.description: Marquis of Pombal's modernisation: expulsion of the Jesuits (1759), educational and commercial reforms, the rebuilding of Lisbon with anti-seismic engineering, and the absolutist legacy.

940.name: Peninsular War & Liberal Era
940.description: Napoleon's invasion forced the royal court to flee to Brazil. The Peninsular War, Wellington's campaigns, and the Liberal Wars shaped 19th-century Portugal. The loss of Brazil (1822) and colonial decline led to political instability and eventually the fall of the monarchy.

sub_clusters.name: Peninsular War & Loss of Brazil
sub_clusters.description: Napoleon's invasion (1807), the royal court's flight to Rio de Janeiro, Wellington's Peninsular War campaigns (Lines of Torres Vedras), and the loss of Brazil to independence (1822).
key_events: Royal court flees to Brazil ahead of Napoleon's invasion (1807)
Brazil declares independence from Portugal (7 Sept 1822)

sub_clusters.name: Constitutional Monarchy & Colonial Decline
sub_clusters.description: The Liberal Wars, Regeneration period, the 1890 British Ultimatum over Africa (Pink Map crisis), regicide of Carlos I (1908), and the republican revolution of 5 October 1910.
key_events: Assassination of King Carlos I in Lisbon (1 Feb 1908)
Republican revolution overthrows the monarchy (5 Oct 1910)

950.name: First Republic & Estado Novo
950.description: Portugal's unstable First Republic gave way to military dictatorship and then Salazar's authoritarian Estado Novo (1933–74). The regime maintained the colonial empire through long, brutal wars in Africa that eventually triggered its downfall.

sub_clusters.name: First Republic & Instability
sub_clusters.description: The chaotic First Republic with 45 governments in 16 years, Portugal's WWI participation (Flanders and Africa), the 1926 military coup, and Salazar's rise as finance minister.

sub_clusters.name: Salazar's Estado Novo
sub_clusters.description: António de Oliveira Salazar's corporatist dictatorship, WWII neutrality, the PIDE secret police, enforced backwardness, and the beginning of colonial wars in Angola (1961), Guinea-Bissau, and Mozambique.
key_events: Colonial War begins with the Angola uprising (1961)

sub_clusters.name: Colonial Wars & the Regime's Final Years
sub_clusters.description: Marcelo Caetano's failed liberalisation after Salazar's incapacitation (1968), the escalating colonial wars draining the country, and the growing military disaffection that led to the Carnation Revolution.

950.name: Carnation Revolution (1974)
950.description: On 25 April 1974, the Movimento das Forças Armadas overthrew the Estado Novo in a nearly bloodless coup, with soldiers placing carnations in their rifle barrels. The revolution ended Europe's longest dictatorship and triggered rapid decolonisation.

sub_clusters.name: 25 April Revolution & PREC
sub_clusters.description: The military coup of 25 April 1974, the Processo Revolucionário Em Curso (PREC) – the turbulent revolutionary period with nationalisations, agrarian reform, and attempted counter-coups – and the 1976 Constitution establishing democracy.
key_events: Carnation Revolution overthrows the Estado Novo (25 April 1974)
New democratic constitution adopted (2 April 1976)

960.name: European Integration & Modernisation
960.description: Democratic Portugal joined the EEC in 1986, triggering dramatic modernisation. Expo '98 in Lisbon symbolised Portugal's transformation, while the return of Macau to China (1999) closed the book on the oldest European colonial empire.

sub_clusters.name: EEC Accession & Modernisation
sub_clusters.description: Democratic consolidation under Mário Soares, EEC accession (1 January 1986), structural fund-driven modernisation, and Portugal's transformation from a backward dictatorship to a modern European democracy.
key_events: Portugal joins the EEC (1 Jan 1986)

sub_clusters.name: Expo '98 & Macau Handover
sub_clusters.description: Lisbon's Expo '98 celebrating the oceans, the handover of Macau to China (20 December 1999) – ending 442 years of Portuguese presence – and euro adoption (2002).
key_events: Handover of Macau to China – end of the Portuguese Empire (20 Dec 1999)

960.name: Contemporary Portugal
960.description: 21st-century Portugal navigated the eurozone debt crisis with austerity and a later 'anti-austerity' recovery, becoming a model for progressive drug policy and renewable energy, while confronting the legacy of colonialism.

sub_clusters.name: Eurozone Crisis & Troika Bailout
sub_clusters.description: The 2011 sovereign debt crisis, the EU-IMF-ECB troika bailout programme, severe austerity measures, emigration, and the 2015 'geringonça' left-wing coalition that pursued an alternative recovery path.

sub_clusters.name: Modern Renaissance & Global Soft Power
sub_clusters.description: Portugal's economic recovery, booming tourism, Lisbon as a European tech hub, the progressive drug decriminalisation model, renewable energy achievements, and reckoning with colonial memory.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
